newsitem.title: USA: Albright plans to visit Middle East in September.
newsitem.headline: Albright plans to visit Middle East in September.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright plans a September trip to the Middle East to focus on speeding Israeli-Palestinian peace talks but with other stops in the region, her spokesman said on Thursday.

The spokesman, James Rubin, also reported that U.S. envoy Dennis Ross believed "there is a good chance" Palestinians would demonstrate sufficient security cooperation soon to enable Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to reverse crippling economic sanctions on the Palestinians.
Ross spent the last five days in the region trying to persuade Israelis and Palestinians to resume cooperating against political violence. He briefed Albright in Washington on Thursday.
"The secretary of state is going to the Middle East soon. I can assure you of that," Rubin told reporters.
"The 'when' is linked to the kind of trip she wants to have and the kind of results that we see in the area of security that we are going to be watching in the coming weeks," he said.

Albright said in a speech on Aug. 6 she was prepared to go to the Middle East at the end of August provided progress was made in improving the security situation after a deterioration culminated in a deadly bombing in Jerusalem on July 30.
"It's possible the trip will not be in August but will be in September," Rubin said. It will be Albright's first visit to the Middle East as secretary of state.

"She is beginning to think a little bit about her schedule ... and exactly what she'll do while she's there. And what we're going to do is watch the results over the coming weeks and make a decision on that basis," Rubin said.
"We have broader interests in the region. We have national security interests that go beyond Israel and the Palestinian Authority," he said.
U.S. officials have said they doubt Albright will travel to Syria. Syrian-Israeli peace talks halted last year.
Rubin said it was unlikely Albright would visit the Gulf states either, although she would discuss on her trip the fourth Middle Eastern economic summit, planned for October in Doha, Qatar.
Saudi Arabia, the Palestinians and the United Arab Emirates say they will boycott the summit if Israel attends. The meeting is an important element in U.S. plans for Middle East peace.
Albright has announced she will attend the summit. Rubin acknowledged there had been troubles with the peace process and said Albright might reconsider her plans after her trip.
He said the trip would focus on a U.S. proposal to speed talks on a final peace between Israel and the Palestinians.

These "final-status" negotiations -- on the future of Jerusalem and the boundaries of Palestinian self-rule areas -- would be undertaken while the two sides were still trying to comply with an interim accord designed to build mutual confidence, officials say.
Interim talks deadlocked in the face of repeated extremist attacks against Israel.
Albright intends to start this accelerated process with her trip. How often she might journey to the region and how long she would continue to play a direct role are uncertain, Rubin said.
During a period when hopes for comprehensive peace were high, former Secretary of State Warren Christopher took a major direct role and made countless trips to the region.
But now that prospects for peace have dimmed, Albright has been more reluctant to jump in. Officials are also concerned about squandering her influence as America's chief diplomat.

Rubin said that if Albright's involvement was not handled correctly, "it will interfere with other priorities that are major and important, like our relations with Europe, NATO enlargement, Bosnia and Europe ... China, South Korea, etc."
Ross is likely to make another trip to the Middle East. That mission will be linked to Albright's trip, and it has not been decided whether it will precede or follow hers, Rubin said.
